summary: Defines an email header field for recording the results of message authentication checks, so filters and mail programs can show or use them. This is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 6577, and it was replaced by RFC 7001.

plainLanguage.summary: After checking whether a letter really came from who it says, a mail server stamps the result on the letter. Later readers can see the stamp. A newer memo replaced it.

questions: how do mail servers record spf and dkim results
what does dkim pass mean in email headers
subtitle: A mail header that records which authentication checks a message passed or failed, for filters and mail programs downstream.

tldr.problem: Mail servers check where a message came from (with methods such as SPF and DKIM), but each method reported its result in its own header, leaving mail programs and filters with no common place to read the outcome.
tldr.mechanism: The Authentication-Results header field names the server that did the checking and lists each method with its result and the message properties it examined. Servers add it at the top and must delete forged copies that claim to come from inside their own trust boundary.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5451 was updated by RFC 6577 and obsoleted by RFC 7001, so the current definition of the header is in the newer document.

facts.label: Initial methods
facts.value: auth, dkim, domainkeys, iprev, sender-id, spf

today: RFC 5451 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 6577 and obsoleted by RFC 7001, so the current definition of the Authentication-Results header is in the newer document.

sections.title: Why a Results Header
sections.content:
This memo defines a header field that presents the results of message authentication in a machine-readable format. It collects the data in one place so that a Mail User Agent (MUA) and downstream filters can make filtering decisions or recommend to the user whether a message's origin is valid. End users are not expected to read it directly; programs use or render it.

The RFC deliberately does not say how the results should be used, because filtering choices and user interfaces are local policy. It also establishes no new requirement on existing protocols or servers, and no requirement on MTAs to reject messages that fail checks.

The methods in common use at the time were SMTP AUTH, DKIM, DomainKeys, Sender-ID and SPF. The older Received-SPF and DomainKey-Status headers each carry only their own method's result, which was not enough for this purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every checker writing its answer in a different place, there is one box on the letter where all the answers go.

sections.title: Trust Boundary and Who Adds the Header
sections.content:
The header is only useful inside a trust boundary: the line between external hosts and internal ones that deliberately provide messaging service for the receiving domain's users. The RFC says a precise definition is not possible, and how trust is obtained is a local matter. The header field has no integrity protection of its own, so its presence must be trusted implicitly.

The checking normally happens at a border MTA (the gateway between the Internet and the organization) or at a delivery MTA. The header presence alone does not mean its data is valid. It means someone upstream asserts validity, so the reader must trust the MTA that added it.

The authserv-id identifies the authenticating service within one administrative domain. It SHOULD be a common token used throughout the domain, such as its DNS domain name. MUAs and downstream filters SHOULD use it to decide whether to use the data.
sections.plainLanguage: A stamp on a letter only counts if you trust whoever stamped it. So the stamp carries the name of the post office that made it.

sections.title: The Authentication-Results Header
sections.content:
The header value is an authserv-id, an optional version, and then a series of method=result statements. Each can carry a reason string and ptype.property=value statements naming what was evaluated. The special value none says no authentication was performed. The header MAY appear more than once in a message, and one header can hold several results.

The ptype is one of smtp (a parameter of an SMTP command), header (a message header field), body (something in the body) or policy (another property evaluated by the receiving MTA).

Result values are defined per method. For DKIM and DomainKeys they are none, pass, fail, policy, neutral, temperror and permerror. SPF and Sender-ID also use hardfail and softfail. SMTP AUTH uses none, pass, fail, temperror and permerror.

The temperror result means a likely transient error, so a later attempt may succeed. The permerror result means an unrecoverable error.
sections.plainLanguage: The stamp says who made it, which test they ran, and what happened, such as passed, failed, or could not tell yet.

sections.title: Methods, Extensions and iprev
sections.content:
The initial method identifiers are auth, dkim, domainkeys, sender-id and spf, plus a new method called iprev. The iprev method looks up the connecting client's IP address to find names (a PTR query), then looks up each name's addresses (A and AAAA queries). It passes if the client's address appears among them. Agents MUST limit how many names they evaluate, and the RFC mentions SPF's limit of 10 as an example.

The RFC is cautious about this test: it notes the reliability debate and says reverse DNS guidance recommends against using it for authentication or security. Its inclusion is not an endorsement.

New methods and result codes not starting with x- MUST be registered with IANA and published in an RFC. Names starting with x- are experimental and never standardized. Production systems SHOULD ignore or delete headers containing them.
sections.plainLanguage: New kinds of checks can be added later. Trial checks get a special label so nobody mistakes them for official ones.

sections.title: Adding, Reading and Removing the Header
sections.content:
An MTA that does one or more authentication tests MUST add the header, either once per test or once with all results, and MUST NOT add a result to an existing header. The header SHOULD go at the top, above other trace fields. The order of methods MUST NOT be read as a ranking of their strength.

MUAs and downstream filters SHOULD NOT interpret the header unless the user or administrator turns that on, and SHOULD NOT interpret it unless the authserv-id is one used within their own domain. They MUST ignore unknown results, unknown ptypes and unsupported methods.

For security, an MTA MUST delete any instance of the header that claims to have been added inside its trust boundary and did not come from another trusted MTA. A border MTA MAY remove all instances, or allow a list of trusted external authenticators. If local policy rejects a message on a hard failure, the border MTA SHOULD reject it during SMTP rather than adding the header, to avoid sending a bounce to a forged sender.
sections.plainLanguage: Each trusted post office adds its own stamp at the top, and throws away any stamp that pretends to be one of its own but was not.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main risk is a forged header. An attacker could add a header using a receiving domain's name as the authserv-id, claiming the message was authenticated. If a non-conformant MTA does not strip it, a mail program might trust it. That is why MUAs should not process the header by default.

The RFC lists possible protections, such as signing the header with DKIM, but says specifying one mechanism is not appropriate for this memo. A pass result also does not make a message trustworthy: spam signed by its own sender can pass DKIM.

Other risks covered include reordering of header fields by some MTAs, denial of service through unbounded reverse-DNS lookups, backscatter from late rejections, stale lists of internal MTAs, attacks on the underlying methods, intentionally malformed or oversized headers, compromised internal hosts, and copies inside encapsulated message/rfc822 attachments, which MUAs SHOULD ignore.
sections.plainLanguage: A cheater might forge a stamp, so mail programs should only trust stamps from post offices they know, and even a good stamp does not prove the letter is nice.

viz.caption: THE FORMAL SYNTAX, ABBREVIATED FROM SECTION 2.2

data.title: Authentication-Results (ABNF)
data.code:
authres-header = "Authentication-Results:" [CFWS] authserv-id
         [ CFWS version ]
         ( [CFWS] ";" [CFWS] "none" / 1*resinfo ) [CFWS] CRLF

resinfo    = [CFWS] ";" methodspec [ CFWS reasonspec ]
             *( CFWS propspec )
methodspec = [CFWS] method [CFWS] "=" [CFWS] result
ptype      = "smtp" / "header" / "body" / "policy"
